```{r setup}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(fig.width = 7.5, fig.height = 4.2, dpi = 300, dev = "png")
library(dplyr)
library(knitr)
library(ggplot2)
library(tidyr)

repo_root <- if (file.exists("Second Step/results/results_all.csv")) {
  "."
} else if (file.exists("../Second Step/results/results_all.csv")) {
  ".."
} else {
  stop("Cannot locate Second Step/results/results_all.csv")
}

results <- read.csv(file.path(repo_root, "Second Step/results/results_all.csv"),
                    stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
conditions <- read.delim(file.path(repo_root, "conditions.tsv"),
                         stringsAsFactors = FALSE, na.strings = "")

results <- results |>
  mutate(
    arm = sub("_[0-9]+$", "", agent_id),
    arm = factor(arm, levels = conditions$condition),
    years_start = as.integer(years_start),
    years_end = as.integer(years_end),
    year_span = years_end - years_start + 1,
    cov_none = grepl("^none$|^$", tolower(trimws(covariates))),
    est_lc = tolower(trimws(estimator)),
    twfe = grepl("twfe|feols|fixest", est_lc),
    continuous_tx = grepl("continuous", tolower(treatment_definition))
  )

arm_summary <- results |>
  group_by(arm) |>
  summarize(
    n = n(),
    mean_att = mean(att_estimate, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd_att = sd(att_estimate, na.rm = TRUE),
    median_att = median(att_estimate, na.rm = TRUE),
    frac_negative = mean(att_estimate < 0, na.rm = TRUE),
    frac_teen = mean(outcome_variable == "emp_pop_ratio_teen", na.rm = TRUE),
    frac_no_cov = mean(cov_none, na.rm = TRUE),
    frac_twfe = mean(twfe, na.rm = TRUE),
    frac_continuous = mean(continuous_tx, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_start = mean(years_start, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_span = mean(year_span, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

between_arm_ss <- function(values, arms) {
  arms <- droplevels(as.factor(arms))
  overall_mean <- mean(values, na.rm = TRUE)
  arm_means <- tapply(values, arms, mean, na.rm = TRUE)
  arm_counts <- table(arms)
  sum(arm_counts[names(arm_means)] * (arm_means - overall_mean)^2)
}

set.seed(42)
obs_stat <- between_arm_ss(results$att_estimate, results$arm)
perm_stats <- replicate(10000, {
  between_arm_ss(results$att_estimate, sample(results$arm))
})
fisher_p <- mean(perm_stats >= obs_stat)

fmt <- function(x, d = 4) sprintf(paste0("%.", d, "f"), x)

# --- Opus 4.6 run (Third Step) ---
results_opus <- read.csv(file.path(repo_root, "Third Step/results_opus46/results_all.csv"),
                         stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

results_opus <- results_opus |>
  mutate(
    arm = sub("_[0-9]+$", "", agent_id),
    arm = factor(arm, levels = conditions$condition),
    years_start = as.integer(years_start),
    years_end = as.integer(years_end),
    year_span = years_end - years_start + 1,
    cov_none = grepl("^none$|^$", tolower(trimws(covariates))),
    est_lc = tolower(trimws(estimator)),
    twfe = grepl("twfe|feols|fixest", est_lc),
    cgbs = grepl("cgbs|continuous.?did|continuous.?treatment.?did", est_lc),
    continuous_tx = grepl("continuous", tolower(treatment_definition))
  )

arm_summary_opus <- results_opus |>
  group_by(arm) |>
  summarize(
    n = n(),
    mean_att = mean(att_estimate, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd_att = sd(att_estimate, na.rm = TRUE),
    median_att = median(att_estimate, na.rm = TRUE),
    frac_negative = mean(att_estimate < 0, na.rm = TRUE),
    frac_teen = mean(outcome_variable == "emp_pop_ratio_teen", na.rm = TRUE),
    frac_no_cov = mean(cov_none, na.rm = TRUE),
    frac_twfe = mean(twfe, na.rm = TRUE),
    frac_cgbs = mean(cgbs, na.rm = TRUE),
    frac_continuous = mean(continuous_tx, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_start = mean(years_start, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_span = mean(year_span, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

set.seed(42)
obs_stat_opus <- between_arm_ss(results_opus$att_estimate, results_opus$arm)
perm_stats_opus <- replicate(10000, {
  between_arm_ss(results_opus$att_estimate, sample(results_opus$arm))
})
fisher_p_opus <- mean(perm_stats_opus >= obs_stat_opus)
kw_opus <- kruskal.test(att_estimate ~ arm, data = results_opus)

pw_opus <- pairwise.wilcox.test(results_opus$att_estimate, results_opus$arm,
                                 p.adjust.method = "none")

# Opus three-arm mapping
results_opus <- results_opus |>
  mutate(
    three_arm = case_when(
      arm == "none" ~ "Control (No Context)",
      as.character(arm) %in% c("null_short", "null_cites") ~ "Null Context",
      as.character(arm) %in% c("negative_short", "negative_cites") ~ "Negative Context",
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    ),
    sig_neg = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(att_pvalue)) < 0.05 & att_estimate < 0
  )

obs_stat_opus_three <- between_arm_ss(results_opus$att_estimate, results_opus$three_arm)
set.seed(42)
perm_stats_opus_three <- replicate(10000, {
  between_arm_ss(results_opus$att_estimate, sample(results_opus$three_arm))
})
fisher_p_opus_three <- mean(perm_stats_opus_three >= obs_stat_opus_three)

# Map five arms → Cunningham's three-arm display
results <- results |>
  mutate(
    three_arm = case_when(
      arm == "none" ~ "Control (No Context)",
      as.character(arm) %in% c("null_short", "null_cites") ~ "Null Context",
      as.character(arm) %in% c("negative_short", "negative_cites") ~ "Negative Context",
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    ),
    sig_neg = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(att_pvalue)) < 0.05 & att_estimate < 0
  )

between_arm_ss_three <- function(df) {
  between_arm_ss(df$att_estimate, df$three_arm)
}

set.seed(42)
df_strip <- results |> filter(is.na(att_estimate) | att_estimate > -0.08)
obs_stat_three <- between_arm_ss_three(df_strip)
perm_stats_three <- replicate(10000, {
  between_arm_ss(df_strip$att_estimate, sample(df_strip$three_arm))
})
fisher_p_three <- mean(perm_stats_three >= obs_stat_three)

substack_colors <- c(
  "Control (No Context)" = "#8A8A8A",
  "Null Context" = "#4F81BD",
  "Negative Context" = "#C0504D"
)

plot_substack_strip <- function(df, title, subtitle, x_limits = NULL) {
  df <- df |>
    mutate(three_arm = factor(three_arm, levels = names(substack_colors)))
  arm_means <- df |>
    group_by(three_arm) |>
    summarize(mean_att = mean(att_estimate), .groups = "drop")

  p <- ggplot(df, aes(x = att_estimate, y = three_arm, color = three_arm)) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linewidth = 0.35, color = "black") +
    geom_point(
      alpha = 0.55, size = 2.4,
      position = position_jitter(height = 0.14, seed = 42)
    ) +
    geom_point(
      data = arm_means,
      aes(x = mean_att, y = three_arm),
      inherit.aes = FALSE,
      shape = 18, size = 3.8, color = "black"
    ) +
    scale_color_manual(values = substack_colors) +
    labs(title = title, subtitle = subtitle, x = "ATT Estimate", y = NULL) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
    theme(
      legend.position = "none",
      panel.grid.major.y = element_line(color = "grey88", linewidth = 0.3),
      panel.grid.major.x = element_line(color = "grey88", linewidth = 0.3),
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
      plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12, hjust = 0),
      plot.subtitle = element_text(color = "grey35", size = 9, hjust = 0),
      axis.text.y = element_text(size = 10)
    )
  if (!is.null(x_limits)) p <- p + coord_cartesian(xlim = x_limits)
  p
}

summarize_negative <- function(df, label) {
  tibble(
    Group = label,
    n = nrow(df),
    `Mean estimate` = fmt(mean(df$att_estimate), 3),
    `25th / 75th pctile` = sprintf(
      "%s / %s",
      fmt(quantile(df$att_estimate, 0.25), 3),
      fmt(quantile(df$att_estimate, 0.75), 3)
    ),
    Median = fmt(median(df$att_estimate), 3),
    `Std. deviation` = fmt(sd(df$att_estimate), 3),
    `% sig. (p < 0.05, neg.)` = sprintf(
      "%.0f%% (%d/%d)",
      100 * mean(df$sig_neg, na.rm = TRUE),
      sum(df$sig_neg, na.rm = TRUE),
      nrow(df)
    ),
    `Mean panel length` = sprintf("%.1f yrs", mean(df$year_span, na.rm = TRUE)),
    `% binary / continuous` = sprintf(
      "%.0f%% / %.0f%%",
      100 * mean(!df$continuous_tx, na.rm = TRUE),
      100 * mean(df$continuous_tx, na.rm = TRUE)
    )
  )
}

neg_arm <- results |> filter(grepl("^negative", as.character(arm)))
neg_cs <- neg_arm |> filter(!twfe)
neg_twfe <- neg_arm |> filter(twfe)

substack_compare <- bind_rows(
  tibble(
    Group = "Cunningham Wave 1: negative-CS",
    n = 49L,
    `Mean estimate` = "-0.004",
    `25th / 75th pctile` = "-0.012 / +0.002",
    Median = "-0.009",
    `Std. deviation` = "0.010",
    `% sig. (p < 0.05, neg.)` = "6% (3/49)",
    `Mean panel length` = "17.1 yrs",
    `% binary / continuous` = "100% / 0%"
  ),
  tibble(
    Group = "Cunningham Wave 2: negative-TWFE",
    n = 13L,
    `Mean estimate` = "-0.024",
    `25th / 75th pctile` = "-0.026 / -0.007",
    Median = "-0.019",
    `Std. deviation` = "0.018",
    `% sig. (p < 0.05, neg.)` = "46% (6/13)",
    `Mean panel length` = "21.6 yrs",
    `% binary / continuous` = "31% / 69%"
  ),
  summarize_negative(neg_cs, "Cursor run: negative-CS"),
  summarize_negative(neg_twfe, "Cursor run: negative-TWFE")
)
```

## Executive summary

This report documents a **Cursor SDK** replication of Scott Cunningham's minimum-wage many-analyst experiment described in [Claude Code 45: AI Agents and the Minimum Wage](https://causalinf.substack.com/p/claude-code-45-ai-agents-and-the) (April 29, 2026). The substantive question is whether **literature primes** causally shift autonomous agents' reported average treatment effects (ATTs) on employment, operating through **specification and estimator choices**. Four model runs are complete across three models, including an **instruction-neutralization experiment**.

**Composer-2 results (Second Step):** **250 agents** completed successfully (**50 per condition**). Reported ATT distributions **do not differ significantly across arms** (Fisher omnibus *p* = `r fmt(fisher_p)`). Unlike Cunningham's Wave 2 finding for negatively primed Claude Code agents, **negative-prime arms did not disproportionately adopt TWFE or continuous treatment**; **~96–100%** used Callaway–Sant'Anna-family estimators and **100% binary** treatment definitions (one agent exception). Specification variation therefore resembles Cunningham's **tightly constrained Wave 1** more than his **estimator-discretion Wave 2**.

**Opus 4.6 results (Third Step):** **249 agents** completed (1 failure; **49** in `negative_cites`, **50** in all other arms). In contrast to Composer-2, reported ATT distributions **differ significantly across arms** (Fisher omnibus *p* = `r fmt(fisher_p_opus)`; Kruskal–Wallis *p* = `r fmt(kw_opus$p.value)`). The **`negative_short` arm** is the clear outlier with mean ATT = `r fmt(arm_summary_opus$mean_att[arm_summary_opus$arm == "negative_short"])` and median = `r fmt(arm_summary_opus$median_att[arm_summary_opus$arm == "negative_short"])` (most negative). This arm also shows more **specification diversity**: 3 continuous treatment, 2 CGBS, 1 TWFE — a pattern that **more closely resembles Cunningham's Wave 2** findings.

**Grok 4.6 v1 (full instructions, *N* = 245):** Fisher omnibus *p* < 0.0001; Kruskal–Wallis *p* = 7 × 10⁻¹². **The strongest prime effect of any model.** Both negative arms shift left through outcome variable and control group selection (100% CS, 100% binary). **Grok 4.6 v2 (neutralized instructions, *N* = 243):** CS recipe and recommendations removed from methodology document. **Identical prime effect** (Fisher *p* < 0.0001, 100% CS) — proving CS preference is model-intrinsic, not instruction-driven.

## Research question and design lineage

Cunningham's experiment randomizes **literature context** while holding data and task instructions fixed, inspired by Borjas & Breznau (2026, *Science Advances*), who showed human immigration researchers' priors predicted estimates through specification search. Randomizing the prior via prompt turns association into **experimental evidence**.

In the Substack post, Cunningham reports **300 agent sessions** across **two waves**:

| Wave | Estimator rule | Arms | *N* per arm | Main finding |
|:-----|:---------------|:-----|:------------|:-------------|
| **1** | Callaway–Sant'Anna **only** | Placebo + JEL guide; negative prime; null prime | 50 | ATT distributions **similar** across arms; negative arm slightly lower mean driven by **earlier panel starts** |
| **2** | CS, BJS, or **TWFE** allowed | Same three arms | 50 | **Negative arm only** shifts: **+24 pp TWFE**, longer panels spanning federal MW hikes, **continuous** treatment; **more negative** reported effects |

This repository implements a **fork** of Cunningham's [`mw-analyst-experiment`](https://github.com/scunning1975/mw-analyst-experiment) design, adapted to **Cursor programmatic agents** (`@cursor/sdk`) rather than the original **Claude Code CLI** (`claude -p`) workflow.

## Experimental setup (this repository)

### Platform and launch pipeline

| Component | Role |
|:----------|:-----|
| **`scripts/launch_experiment_cursor.mjs`** | Creates temp workspaces, copies data and markdown instructions, launches local Cursor agents with concurrency control |
| **`CURSOR_API_KEY`** | Cursor User API key (distinct from IDE subscription login) |
| **`scripts/collect_results.sh`** | Aggregates per-agent `results.csv` and `llms.txt` into `Second Step/results/` |
| **`scripts/analyze_results.R`** | Fisher randomization tests, Kruskal–Wallis, specification tables, plots |
| **`scripts/analyze_second_step_detail.R`** | Extended arm summaries, estimator-family breakdown, forest/violin plots → `Second Step/analysis/` |

Default full run: **`N_TOTAL=250`**, **`N_PER_CONDITION=50`**, model configurable via `CURSOR_MODEL`. Completed runs: **`composer-2`** (Second Step), **`opus-4.6`**, **`grok-4.6`** v1 and v2 (Third Step).

### Treatment arms (five conditions)

Defined in `conditions.tsv`:

| Arm ID | Label | Literature file |
|:-------|:------|:------------------|
| `none` | None | *(none)* |
| `null_short` | Null Short | `PRIME_NULL_SHORT.md` |
| `null_cites` | Null Cites | `PRIME_NULL_CITES.md` |
| `negative_short` | Negative Short | `PRIME_NEGATIVE_SHORT.md` |
| `negative_cites` | Negative Cites | `PRIME_NEGATIVE_CITES.md` |

**Design differences from Cunningham (Substack):**

1. **Five arms** instead of three — splits null and negative primes into **brief** vs **citation-rich** versions, plus a **no-literature** control (`none`) rather than a placebo that still receives the JEL practitioner's guide summary.
2. **Methodology document** — agents read `DID_METHODOLOGY.md` (Baker et al. practitioner guide content) rather than receiving it as the *only* distinguishing feature of a "placebo" arm. All arms receive the same methodology reference.
3. **Estimator discretion from the start (second wave)** — active `DID_METHODOLOGY.md` explicitly **allows TWFE, BJS-style, and CS** estimators (Section "Choice of Estimator"), analogous to Cunningham's **Wave 2** protocol. The frozen first-wave snapshot in `First Step/` did **not** include this permissive language.
4. **Pre-aggregated data** — agents receive `data/agent_panel_essential.csv` (state × year panel, 1990–2022) rather than rebuilding from raw IPUMS CPS microdata, QCEW, and Zipperer MW series.

### Agent task

Each agent must produce:

- **`results.csv`** — one row with outcome, treatment definition, estimator, sample window, ATT point estimate, SE, CI, etc.
- **`llms.txt`** — structured narrative of design choices and interpretation

Agents have full discretion over outcome variable, sample years, treatment definition (binary vs continuous), comparison group, covariates, and estimator — subject to the methodology reference.

### Data

State-level annual panel (`agent_panel_essential.csv`):

- **51 units** (50 states + DC), **1990–2022**
- CPS-derived employment-to-population ratios (teen, young adult, low education, etc.)
- QCEW industry employment and wages
- Zipperer/EPI effective minimum wage and change indicators

## Key results — Composer-2 run (Second Step, *N* = 250)

```{r arm-table}
arm_summary |>
  transmute(
    Arm = as.character(arm),
    `N` = n,
    `Mean ATT` = fmt(mean_att),
    `SD ATT` = fmt(sd_att),
    `Median ATT` = fmt(median_att),
    `% negative` = fmt(100 * frac_negative, 1),
    `% teen outcome` = fmt(100 * frac_teen, 1),
    `% no covariates` = fmt(100 * frac_no_cov, 1),
    `% TWFE` = fmt(100 * frac_twfe, 1),
    `Mean start year` = fmt(mean_start, 0),
    `Mean span (yrs)` = fmt(mean_span, 1)
  ) |>
  kable(booktabs = TRUE, align = c("l", rep("r", 10)))
```

### Randomization inference

```{r inference}
kw <- kruskal.test(att_estimate ~ arm, data = results)
cat(sprintf("- **Fisher omnibus** (between-arm SS, 10,000 permutations): observed = %s, *p* = %s\n",
            fmt(obs_stat), fmt(fisher_p)))
cat(sprintf("- **Kruskal–Wallis** (all five arms): chi-squared = %s, *p* = %s\n",
            fmt(kw$statistic), fmt(kw$p.value)))
```

**Planned contrasts** (null vs negative, short and cites versions):

| Contrast | Difference (null − negative) | *p* (two-sided) |
|:---------|:----------------------------:|:----------------:|
| Null Short − Negative Short | −0.0019 | 0.512 |
| Null Cites − Negative Cites | +0.0051 | 0.207 |

Neither contrast is significant. The omnibus test fails to reject the sharp null that **condition labels are exchangeable** with respect to reported ATT.

### Specification choices

**Outcome variable:** **498/250 ≈ 99.6%** chose `emp_pop_ratio_teen` (one agent in `negative_short` used `emp_pop_ratio_lt_hs`). Cunningham's Wave 1 reported **97% teen** — very similar convergence.

**Estimator family:** **247/250 (98.8%)** used Callaway–Sant'Anna-family estimators. Only **3 agents** used TWFE-like estimators: 1 in `null_short`, 2 in `negative_short`. **No arm exceeded 4% TWFE.** Chi-squared test of estimator family × arm: *p* ≈ 0.52.

**Treatment definition:** **249/250 binary**; one `negative_short` agent used a custom binary definition keyed to federal-floor binding. **Zero continuous** minimum-wage treatment measures — unlike Cunningham's Wave 2 negative arm (>67% continuous among TWFE users).

**Covariates:** Roughly **42–66%** of agents per arm reported **no covariates** (unconditional PT). Cunningham's Wave 1 reported **0% covariate use** — this Cursor run shows **more conditioning**, but not differentially by arm.

**Sample windows:** Mean panel length **23–27 years** across arms; mean start years **1995–1999**. Cunningham's Wave 1 negative CS agents averaged **17.1 years** with earlier starts driving more negative means; here, **`null_cites` starts latest (1999)** but **`negative_cites` has the longest span (27.4 years)** without a clear negative-arm panel-length advantage.

**Event studies:** **≥98%** per arm produced an event study.

## Substack-style figures (side-by-side with Cunningham)

The figures below mirror the layout in [Cunningham's Substack post](https://causalinf.substack.com/p/claude-code-45-ai-agents-and-the): horizontal strip plots with jittered agent-level ATTs, black diamonds for arm means, and a vertical zero line. Five experimental arms are collapsed to Cunningham's three display groups: **`none` → Control**, **`null_short` + `null_cites` → Null Context**, **`negative_short` + `negative_cites` → Negative Context**.

### Wave 1 analogue — similar distributions across arms

Cunningham's Wave 1 (CS-only) found overlapping ATT distributions across control, null, and negative arms. The Cursor replication shows the same pattern when mapped to three arms: Fisher *p* = `r fmt(fisher_p_three)` (three-arm omnibus, 10,000 permutations).

```{r fig-substack-wave1, fig.cap="Substack-style strip plot (Wave 1 analogue). Each dot is one agent's reported ATT; diamonds are arm means. Five arms mapped to three display groups."}
plot_substack_strip(
  df_strip,
  title = sprintf("%d Cursor agents, same data, same question — different answers", nrow(df_strip)),
  subtitle = sprintf(
    "Each dot is one agent's ATT. Diamonds = arm means. Fisher p = %s (three arms).",
    fmt(fisher_p_three)
  ),
  x_limits = c(-0.025, 0.015)
)
```

### Wave 2 analogue — no negative-arm left shift

Cunningham's Wave 2 strip plot shows the negative-context arm shifted substantially left (Fisher *p* < 0.0001 in his slides). The Cursor run used Wave-2-style estimator rules from the start (TWFE allowed), but **does not** reproduce that separation: negative-context means overlap null and control.

```{r fig-substack-wave2, fig.cap="Substack-style strip plot (Wave 2 analogue). Wider x-axis as in Cunningham's Wave 2 figure; negative arm does not separate."}
plot_substack_strip(
  df_strip,
  title = "Cursor run (TWFE allowed): Negative-context agents do not produce more negative reported ATTs",
  subtitle = sprintf(
    "Mapped to Cunningham's three arms. Fisher p = %s. Diamonds = arm means.",
    fmt(fisher_p_three)
  ),
  x_limits = c(-0.06, 0.02)
)
```

### Negative-arm CS vs TWFE comparison table

Cunningham's Substack table contrasts **negative-primed agents who stayed on Callaway–Sant'Anna** (Wave 1, *n* = 49) with **negative-primed agents who switched to TWFE** (Wave 2, *n* = 13). The Cursor run had only **2** negative-arm TWFE agents, so the TWFE row is illustrative rather than a stable subgroup.

```{r substack-table}
substack_compare |>
  kable(
    booktabs = TRUE,
    align = c("l", "c", rep("r", 7)),
    caption = "Negative-context agents: Cunningham (Substack) vs Cursor replication."
  )
```

**Reading the table:** Cunningham's Wave 2 TWFE subgroup shows a **6× more negative** mean ATT (−0.024 vs −0.004), longer panels (21.6 vs 17.1 years), and **69% continuous** treatment. The Cursor negative-CS subgroup (*n* = 98) closely matches Cunningham's Wave 1 negative-CS mean (−0.005 vs −0.004) but with more covariate use and longer panels overall. The two Cursor negative-TWFE agents are both significant and negative, but *n* = 2 is too small to infer a Wave 2-style mechanism.

## Agent configuration audit: CLAUDE.md, skills, and what agents actually see

A natural hypothesis for the missing Wave 2 TWFE shift is that **Cunningham's Claude Code agents inherited global project memory or skills** that your Cursor agents did not. We audited both setups.

### What the public repositories actually ship to each agent

Neither Cunningham's [`mw-analyst-experiment`](https://github.com/scunning1975/mw-analyst-experiment) nor this repo copies **`CLAUDE.md`**, **`AGENTS.md`**, or **skill files** into agent workspaces. Both launchers build an isolated temp directory containing only:

| File | Cunningham (Claude Code) | This repo (Cursor SDK) |
|:-----|:-------------------------|:-----------------------|
| `agent_panel_essential.csv` | Yes | Yes |
| `DATA_DICTIONARY.md` | Yes | Yes |
| `DID_METHODOLOGY.md` | Yes | Yes |
| `INSTRUCTIONS_SHARED.md` | Yes | Yes |
| `LITERATURE_CONTEXT.md` | Null or negative arms only | Primed arms only (renamed from `PRIME_*.md`) |
| `prompt.txt` | Yes | Yes |

**No `CLAUDE.md` or `.claude/skills/` appear in either experiment repository** or in the workspace copy step. Cunningham's MixtapeTools [`claude/CLAUDE.md`](https://github.com/scunning1975/MixtapeTools/blob/main/claude/CLAUDE.md) is a **template** for interactive research projects, not part of the batch experiment payload.

### The critical runtime difference: ambient settings loading

Despite identical workspace files, the **agent runtimes differ in what they load from outside the temp folder**:

| Setting layer | Cunningham (`claude -p` from `/tmp/mw_agent_*`) | This repo (`launch_experiment_cursor.mjs`) |
|:--------------|:--------------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------|
| Workspace markdown | 4–5 copied files only | Same |
| User `CLAUDE.md` | **Loaded by default** (Claude Code memory hierarchy) if present at `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` | **Not loaded** |
| Project rules / skills | **Available** if installed globally or in parent dirs | **Explicitly disabled** via `settingSources: []` |
| Cursor user rules (`~/.cursor/rules/`) | N/A | **Not loaded** into SDK agents |

Relevant launcher code:

```201:201:scripts/launch_experiment_cursor.mjs
      local: { cwd: workDir, settingSources: [] },
```

The Cursor SDK documents this as intentional: `settingSources: []` means **"inline config only"** — the agent sees the prompt and workspace files, nothing else ([SDK skill](https://cursor.com/docs/sdk/typescript)). That is appropriate for a clean experiment, but it is **stricter isolation than Claude Code's default**.

On this machine, `~/.claude/` contains session caches only (no installed `CLAUDE.md` or skills), and `~/.cursor/rules/` has a single AI-acknowledgment rule — so **you are not leaving obvious global econometric skills on the table locally**. Cunningham's Georgetown machine may differ: his MixtapeTools repo ships skills like **`referee2`** (econometric audit), **`blindspot`**, and **`split-pdf`**, typically installed to `~/.claude/skills/` or `~/mixtapetools/.claude/skills/` for interactive Claude Code work. Those skills were **not** part of the published experiment repo, and batch agents are launched with `--allowedTools "Read,Write,Bash"` only — they cannot invoke `/referee2` unless they somehow know to.

**Bottom line on skills:** There is no evidence that Cunningham's **published** Wave 2 protocol depended on skill files in the workspace. Any skill effect would have to come from **global Claude Code memory on his machine**, which we cannot observe. Your Cursor runs are **more aggressively sandboxed**, which would suppress such effects if they existed — but cannot by itself explain why your agents **over-comply** with Callaway–Sant'Anna rather than **under-comply** toward TWFE.

### Instruction-file differences that *are* observable (and matter more than CLAUDE.md)

These differences live in the copied markdown, not in CLAUDE.md:

| Layer | Cunningham Wave 1 (public GitHub) | Cunningham Wave 2 (Substack) | This Cursor run |
|:------|:----------------------------------|:-----------------------------|:----------------|
| **TWFE in `DID_METHODOLOGY.md`** | Section 3: **"Do not use TWFE"** | Same JEL text but **CS / BJS / TWFE allowed** | Section 3: caveats only; **Choice of Estimator** permits TWFE |
| **Arms** | 3 (`none`, `null`, `negative`) | Same | **5** (adds short vs cites splits) |
| **Control / placebo** | All arms get JEL; `none` = no literature prime | Same | All arms get `DID_METHODOLOGY.md`; `none` = no `LITERATURE_CONTEXT.md` |
| **Negative prime** | Single long `PRIME_NEGATIVE.md` (4 cited papers) | Same text family | `PRIME_NEGATIVE_SHORT.md` (2 sentences) + `PRIME_NEGATIVE_CITES.md` (4 papers, shorter prose) |
| **`results.csv` estimator field** | `"callaway_santanna" or "cgbs_continuous" or other` | Same schema | **Explicitly lists `"twfe"`** as a named option |
| **Pre-registration "no menu" principle** | Agents should not get a checklist of choices | Same philosophy | Listing `twfe` in deliverables schema is a mild menu cue (but did not trigger adoption) |

The Wave 2 behavioral shift Cunningham documents — negative arm **+24 pp TWFE**, **69% continuous treatment**, longer panels — occurred when he **relaxed** the TWFE ban in `DID_METHODOLOGY.md`. Your active protocol is already Wave-2-like on paper, yet **98.8%** of agents still used Callaway–Sant'Anna and **0%** used continuous treatment. The instruction diff therefore **cannot** be the whole story: your agents had permission to TWFE and largely declined.

Sample negative-prime agent narrative (`negative_short_001`) shows the typical path: read negative literature → define binary staggered treatment → **`att_gt()` with DR / not-yet-treated** → report ATT. No transcript evidence of TWFE experimentation followed by promotion (Cunningham's Wave 2 mechanism).

### Most plausible explanations (ranked)

1. **Model / platform behavior (largest)** — Cursor `composer-2` agents treat `DID_METHODOLOGY.md` Section 3 TWFE caveats as binding guidance and default to `did::att_gt()`, even when TWFE is permitted. Cunningham's Claude Code sessions (pinned Claude model) appear more willing to treat TWFE as a **robustness fallback** when CS estimates contradict assigned literature.

2. **Sequential wave context (Cunningham only)** — Wave 2 is a **protocol change** on the same Substack storyline; agents are still fresh instances, but Cunningham's **wording change** (removing the hard TWFE ban) may interact with Claude's prior training on minimum-wage TWFE papers cited in the negative prime. Your run jumped straight to the permissive protocol without a CS-only baseline wave in the same pipeline.

3. **Prime packaging** — Cunningham's single long negative prime foregrounds four classic **panel FE** studies. Your `negative_short` arm is only two sentences; `negative_cites` cites the same authors but with less rhetorical emphasis on estimator choice. Neither matches Cunningham's exact prime text.

4. **Ambient Claude memory (unobserved, Cunningham-side only)** — If his batch runs inherit a user-level `CLAUDE.md` emphasizing "when CS fails or contradicts literature, try alternative estimators," that could nudge Wave 2 behavior. Your `settingSources: []` would block the Cursor analogue even if you had one.

5. **Skills (unlikely for batch runs)** — MixtapeTools skills are built for **interactive** `/referee2`-style audits, not autonomous `-p` batches. No skill files were in either experiment workspace.

### Testable next steps

To separate configuration from model effects:

- **Re-run with `settingSources: ["all"]`** (or copy a minimal project `CLAUDE.md` into each workspace) and compare TWFE adoption rates.
- **Use Cunningham's exact three-arm primes and Wave 2 `DID_METHODOLOGY.md` text** verbatim in the workspace copy step.
- **Run the same launcher with a Claude model via Cursor SDK** (if available on your account) holding instructions fixed.
- **Inspect agent logs** for TWFE trials that were abandoned (Cunningham reports negative-arm agents experiment with TWFE then promote it; your logs would show whether that trial phase is missing entirely).

## Key results — Opus 4.6 run (Third Step, *N* = 249)

The Opus 4.6 run used the **identical experimental protocol, data, instructions, and five-arm design** as the Composer-2 Second Step. The only difference is the underlying AI model: `claude-opus-4-6` via Cursor SDK. One agent failed to return a usable `results.csv`, yielding 249 completed analyses.

### Arm-level ATT summary (Opus 4.6)

```{r arm-table-opus}
arm_summary_opus |>
  transmute(
    Arm = as.character(arm),
    `N` = n,
    `Mean ATT` = fmt(mean_att),
    `SD ATT` = fmt(sd_att),
    `Median ATT` = fmt(median_att),
    `% negative` = fmt(100 * frac_negative, 1),
    `% teen outcome` = fmt(100 * frac_teen, 1),
    `% no covariates` = fmt(100 * frac_no_cov, 1),
    `% TWFE` = fmt(100 * frac_twfe, 1),
    `% continuous Tx` = fmt(100 * frac_continuous, 1),
    `Mean span (yrs)` = fmt(mean_span, 1)
  ) |>
  kable(booktabs = TRUE, align = c("l", rep("r", 10)),
        caption = "Opus 4.6 arm-level summary (Third Step, N = 249).")
```

### Randomization inference (Opus 4.6)

```{r inference-opus}
cat(sprintf("- **Fisher omnibus** (between-arm SS, 10,000 permutations): observed = %s, *p* = %s\n",
            fmt(obs_stat_opus), fmt(fisher_p_opus)))
cat(sprintf("- **Kruskal–Wallis** (all five arms): chi-squared = %s, *p* = %s\n",
            fmt(kw_opus$statistic), fmt(kw_opus$p.value)))
```

Unlike the Composer-2 run, **the Opus 4.6 omnibus tests reject the sharp null** that condition labels are exchangeable with respect to reported ATT. The signal is driven by the `negative_short` arm.

**Pairwise Wilcoxon rank-sum tests** (unadjusted):

```{r pairwise-opus}
pw_df <- tibble(
  Comparison = paste(rep(rownames(pw_opus$p.value), each = ncol(pw_opus$p.value)),
                     "vs",
                     rep(colnames(pw_opus$p.value), times = nrow(pw_opus$p.value))),
  p_value = as.vector(as.matrix(pw_opus$p.value))
) |>
  filter(!is.na(p_value)) |>
  arrange(p_value) |>
  mutate(p_value = fmt(p_value))
kable(pw_df, booktabs = TRUE, col.names = c("Comparison", "p-value"),
      caption = "Pairwise Wilcoxon rank-sum tests (Opus 4.6 run, unadjusted).")
```

The strongest pairwise contrast is `null_cites` vs `negative_short` (*p* ≈ 0.024), consistent with the `negative_short` arm producing distinctly more negative ATTs.

### Three-arm view (Opus 4.6)

Mapping to Cunningham's three display groups: Fisher *p* = `r fmt(fisher_p_opus_three)` (three-arm omnibus). While the five-arm test is significant, the three-arm grouping dilutes the `negative_short` signal by pooling it with `negative_cites` (which behaves more like the null arms).

```{r fig-substack-opus, fig.cap="Opus 4.6 strip plot (Cunningham three-arm mapping). Diamonds = arm means."}
plot_substack_strip(
  results_opus |> filter(is.na(att_estimate) | att_estimate > -0.08),
  title = sprintf("%d Opus 4.6 agents — negative_short arm shifts left", nrow(results_opus)),
  subtitle = sprintf(
    "Each dot = one agent's ATT. Diamonds = arm means. Fisher p = %s (three arms), %s (five arms).",
    fmt(fisher_p_opus_three), fmt(fisher_p_opus)
  ),
  x_limits = c(-0.06, 0.04)
)
```

```{r fig-att-opus, fig.cap="Distribution of reported ATT estimates by treatment arm — Opus 4.6 (N = 249)."}
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(repo_root, "Third Step/results_opus46/att_by_arm.png"))
```

### Specification patterns (Opus 4.6)

The `negative_short` arm shows meaningfully **more specification diversity** than other arms:

| Feature | `negative_short` (n=50) | Other arms (n=199) |
|:--------|:-----------------------:|:-------------------:|
| Continuous treatment | **3 (6%)** | 0 (0%) |
| CGBS / continuous DiD estimator | **2 (4%)** | 0 (0%) |
| TWFE estimator | **1 (2%)** | 0 (0%) |
| Never-treated control group | **11 (22%)** | Lower fraction |
| Callaway–Sant'Anna | ~44 (~88%) | ~199 (~100%) |

This pattern is reminiscent of Cunningham's **Wave 2 finding**: negatively primed agents exercising more estimator and treatment-definition discretion, producing more diverse specifications and more negative ATTs.

- **Treatment definition × arm:** Fisher exact test *p* ≈ 0.051 (borderline).
- **Estimator family × arm:** The concentration of non-CS estimators in `negative_short` is notable given that all other arms are nearly 100% CS.

### Why `negative_short` but not `negative_cites`?

The asymmetry between the two negative-prime arms is notable. The **short** prime is a concise two-sentence assertion that minimum wages reduce employment, without citations or caveats. The **cites** version includes the same claim but embedded in academic references. One hypothesis: the **direct, unqualified assertion** may be more effective at overriding agents' default methodological choices than a citation-rich version that the agent may interpret as requiring more careful engagement with the evidence. This parallels findings in human psychology about the persuasive power of simple, confident messages versus complex, nuanced ones.

## Grok 4.6 results

```{r grok-setup}
# --- Grok 4.6 v1 ---
results_grok <- read.csv(
  file.path(repo_root, "Third Step/results_grok46/results_all.csv"),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
) |>
  mutate(
    arm = sub("_[0-9]+$", "", agent_id),
    arm = factor(arm, levels = conditions$condition),
    years_start = as.integer(years_start), years_end = as.integer(years_end),
    year_span = years_end - years_start + 1,
    est_lc = tolower(trimws(estimator)),
    twfe = grepl("twfe|feols|fixest", est_lc),
    continuous_tx = grepl("continuous", tolower(treatment_definition)),
    model = "grok-4.6"
  )

arm_summary_grok <- results_grok |>
  group_by(arm) |>
  summarize(n = n(), mean_att = mean(att_estimate, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd_att = sd(att_estimate, na.rm = TRUE),
    median_att = median(att_estimate, na.rm = TRUE),
    frac_negative = mean(att_estimate < 0, na.rm = TRUE),
    frac_teen = mean(outcome_variable == "emp_pop_ratio_teen", na.rm = TRUE),
    frac_twfe = mean(twfe, na.rm = TRUE),
    frac_continuous = mean(continuous_tx, na.rm = TRUE),
    frac_nevertreated = mean(grepl("never", tolower(control_group)), na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop")

set.seed(42)
obs_stat_grok <- between_arm_ss(results_grok$att_estimate, results_grok$arm)
fisher_p_grok <- mean(replicate(10000, between_arm_ss(results_grok$att_estimate, sample(results_grok$arm))) >= obs_stat_grok)
kw_grok <- kruskal.test(att_estimate ~ arm, data = results_grok)

# --- Grok 4.6 v2 (neutralized) ---
results_grok2 <- read.csv(
  file.path(repo_root, "Third Step/results_grok46_v2/results_all.csv"),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
) |>
  mutate(
    arm = sub("_[0-9]+$", "", agent_id),
    arm = factor(arm, levels = conditions$condition),
    years_start = as.integer(years_start), years_end = as.integer(years_end),
    year_span = years_end - years_start + 1,
    est_lc = tolower(trimws(estimator)),
    twfe = grepl("twfe|feols|fixest", est_lc),
    continuous_tx = grepl("continuous", tolower(treatment_definition)),
    model = "grok-4.6-v2"
  )

arm_summary_grok2 <- results_grok2 |>
  group_by(arm) |>
  summarize(n = n(), mean_att = mean(att_estimate, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd_att = sd(att_estimate, na.rm = TRUE),
    median_att = median(att_estimate, na.rm = TRUE),
    frac_negative = mean(att_estimate < 0, na.rm = TRUE),
    frac_teen = mean(outcome_variable == "emp_pop_ratio_teen", na.rm = TRUE),
    frac_twfe = mean(twfe, na.rm = TRUE),
    frac_continuous = mean(continuous_tx, na.rm = TRUE),
    frac_nevertreated = mean(grepl("never", tolower(control_group)), na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop")

set.seed(42)
obs_stat_grok2 <- between_arm_ss(results_grok2$att_estimate, results_grok2$arm)
fisher_p_grok2 <- mean(replicate(10000, between_arm_ss(results_grok2$att_estimate, sample(results_grok2$arm))) >= obs_stat_grok2)
kw_grok2 <- kruskal.test(att_estimate ~ arm, data = results_grok2)
```

### Grok 4.6 v1 (full instructions, *N* = `r nrow(results_grok)`)

Grok 4.6 shows the **strongest prime effect of any model tested**:

```{r grok-arm-table}
arm_summary_grok |>
  transmute(Arm = as.character(arm), N = n,
    `Mean ATT` = fmt(mean_att), SD = fmt(sd_att), Median = fmt(median_att),
    `% neg.` = fmt(100 * frac_negative, 1),
    `% teen` = fmt(100 * frac_teen, 1),
    `% nevertreated` = fmt(100 * frac_nevertreated, 1)) |>
  kable(booktabs = TRUE, caption = "Grok 4.6 v1 arm-level summary.")
```

- **Fisher omnibus** *p* = `r fmt(fisher_p_grok)` · **Kruskal–Wallis** *p* = `r sprintf("%.1e", kw_grok$p.value)`
- Both planned contrasts significant: Null Short − Neg Short *p* < 0.0001; Null Cites − Neg Cites *p* < 0.001

**Mechanism:** Unlike Opus 4.6, Grok agents stayed **100% on Callaway–Sant'Anna** with **100% binary treatment**. The prime effect operates through **outcome variable selection** (`negative_short`: 17% non-teen outcomes vs 0% in other arms; χ² *p* = 0.001) and **control group choice** (`negative_short`: 25% nevertreated vs 2–6% in null/control arms).

### Grok 4.6 v2 (neutralized instructions, *N* = `r nrow(results_grok2)`)

To test whether the CS step-by-step recipe in `DID_METHODOLOGY.md` was driving estimator choice, we ran a second Grok 4.6 wave after removing the `did` package syntax, practical checklist, and not-yet-treated recommendation.

```{r grok2-arm-table}
arm_summary_grok2 |>
  transmute(Arm = as.character(arm), N = n,
    `Mean ATT` = fmt(mean_att), SD = fmt(sd_att), Median = fmt(median_att),
    `% teen` = fmt(100 * frac_teen, 1),
    `% nevertreated` = fmt(100 * frac_nevertreated, 1)) |>
  kable(booktabs = TRUE, caption = "Grok 4.6 v2 (neutralized instructions) arm-level summary.")
```

- **Fisher omnibus** *p* = `r fmt(fisher_p_grok2)` · **Kruskal–Wallis** *p* = `r sprintf("%.1e", kw_grok2$p.value)`
- **100% Callaway–Sant'Anna**, **100% binary** — identical to v1 despite removing the recipe.
- Prime effect magnitude essentially unchanged: `negative_short` mean ATT = `r fmt(arm_summary_grok2$mean_att[arm_summary_grok2$arm == "negative_short"])` (v2) vs `r fmt(arm_summary_grok$mean_att[arm_summary_grok$arm == "negative_short"])` (v1).

**Key finding:** Removing the CS cookbook had **no effect** on estimator adoption. The Callaway–Sant'Anna preference is baked into model training. Removing the not-yet-treated recommendation **did shift control group choices** in non-primed arms (`none`: 90% nevertreated in v2 vs ~4% in v1), but this did not attenuate the prime effect.

## Cross-model comparison

```{r cross-omnibus-all}
cross_omnibus <- tibble(
  Model = c("Composer-2", "Opus 4.6", "Grok 4.6 v1", "Grok 4.6 v2 (neutralized)"),
  N = c(nrow(results), nrow(results_opus), nrow(results_grok), nrow(results_grok2)),
  `Fisher p` = c(fmt(fisher_p), fmt(fisher_p_opus), fmt(fisher_p_grok), fmt(fisher_p_grok2)),
  `KW p` = c(fmt(kw$p.value), fmt(kw_opus$p.value),
             sprintf("%.1e", kw_grok$p.value), sprintf("%.1e", kw_grok2$p.value)),
  `Primary channel` = c("—", "Estimator/treatment", "Outcome + control", "Outcome + control"),
  `Significant?` = c("No", "Yes", "Yes", "Yes")
)
kable(cross_omnibus, booktabs = TRUE, align = c("l", "r", "r", "r", "l", "c"),
      caption = "Omnibus test comparison across all model runs.")
```

The cross-model comparison reveals three key findings:

1. **Model choice is a first-order moderator.** The same protocol yields null results with `composer-2`, moderate effects with `opus-4.6`, and strong effects with `grok-4.6`.
2. **The mechanism varies by model.** Opus shifts through estimator/treatment switching (closer to Cunningham's Wave 2); Grok shifts through outcome variable and control group selection — a **novel channel** not documented in Cunningham's work.
3. **Instructional scaffolding does not drive estimator choice.** The Grok v1 → v2 comparison demonstrates that removing the CS recipe changes nothing about estimator adoption or prime effect magnitude.

## Comparison to Cunningham (2026 Substack)

### What replicates

| Finding | Cunningham | Composer-2 | Opus 4.6 | Grok 4.6 |
|:--------|:-----------|:-----------|:---------|:---------|
| Converge on **teen employment** | ~97% | ~99.6% | ~99% | ~83% (neg arms diversify) |
| **ATT similar** under narrow estimator choice | Wave 1: large *p* | Fisher *p* = 0.41 | N/A | N/A |
| Default to **CS** | Wave 1: 100% | ~99% | ~96% | **100%** |
| **Negative prime shifts ATTs** | Yes (Wave 2) | **No** | **Partially** | **Strongly** |

### What differs

| Dimension | Cunningham | Composer-2 | Opus 4.6 | Grok 4.6 |
|:----------|:-----------|:-----------|:---------|:---------|
| **Omnibus *p*** | <0.0001 (W2) | 0.41 | **0.001** | **<0.0001** |
| **TWFE shift** | +24 pp neg arm | ≤4%, no effect | 2% in neg\_short | **0%** |
| **Mechanism** | Estimator switch | — | Estimator switch | **Outcome + control** |
| **Continuous Tx** | >67% neg TWFE | 0% | 6% neg\_short | **0%** |
| **Both neg arms shift?** | Yes | No | neg\_short only | **Yes** |

### Interpretation

**Composer-2:** Cunningham's Wave 2 mechanism **does not appear**. Behavior resembles Wave 1's constrained pattern.

**Opus 4.6:** Wave 2 **partially replicates**. The `negative_short` arm shows ATT shifts and specification diversity (TWFE, continuous, CGBS). The short prime format is more effective than citation-rich.

**Grok 4.6:** The **strongest prime effect** of any model, but through a **novel channel** — outcome variable and control group selection rather than estimator switching. Both negative arms shift, and the effect persists identically when the CS recipe is removed from instructions.

**Cross-model synthesis:**

1. **Model is a first-order moderator** — `composer-2` is immune; `opus-4.6` responds moderately; `grok-4.6` responds strongly.
2. **The mechanism varies by model** — Opus mirrors Cunningham's estimator-switching channel; Grok discovers an outcome/control-group channel. Both produce more negative ATTs in negative-primed arms.
3. **Instructional scaffolding does not drive estimator choice** — The Grok v2 experiment (CS recipe removed) shows identical estimator adoption and prime effect magnitude, proving the CS preference comes from model training.
4. **Prime format matters** — Short, assertive primes consistently outperform citation-rich primes across models (`negative_short` > `negative_cites`).
5. **The instruction experiment reveals decomposable effects** — Removing the not-yet-treated recommendation shifts control group choice in *all* arms but does not alter the *between-arm* prime effect. Instructions and primes operate on different specification margins.

Cunningham's deeper point is **strengthened and extended**: priors causally shift agent behavior, but the **channel** depends on the model, and the **magnitude** depends on both model and prime format. The instruction-neutralization result adds a new dimension: some specification defaults are model-intrinsic and cannot be unlocked by changing the methodology document.

## Repository structure and reproducibility

```text
├── First Step/                    # Frozen 150-agent (30×5) first-wave materials
├── Second Step/
│   ├── results/                   # 250-agent Composer-2 outputs
│   └── analysis/                  # Extended tables and figures
├── Third Step/
│   ├── results_opus46/            # 249-agent Opus 4.6 outputs
│   ├── results_grok46/           # 245-agent Grok 4.6 v1 (full instructions)
│   └── results_grok46_v2/        # 243-agent Grok 4.6 v2 (neutralized instructions)
├── data/agent_panel_essential.csv
├── conditions.tsv
├── DID_METHODOLOGY.md
├── INSTRUCTIONS_SHARED.md
├── PRIME_*.md
└── scripts/             # launch, collect, analyze
```

To reproduce analysis from the repo root:

```bash
Rscript scripts/analyze_results.R "Second Step/results"
Rscript scripts/analyze_second_step_detail.R
Rscript scripts/analyze_results.R "Third Step/results_opus46"
Rscript scripts/analyze_results.R "Third Step/results_grok46"
Rscript scripts/analyze_results.R "Third Step/results_grok46_v2"
```

## Limitations

- **Three models tested** (`composer-2`, `opus-4.6`, `grok-4.6`); more models (e.g., GPT-5.6, Fable 5.1) needed to map the full model × prime sensitivity frontier.
- **No transcript-level rhetoric analysis** — Cunningham's confidence-scoring pipeline is not replicated here.
- **Instruction neutralization tested only for Grok** — The same experiment on Opus 4.6 would test whether its estimator-switching channel also persists without the CS recipe.
- **Attrition** — Composer-2: 250/250. Opus 4.6: 249/250. Grok v1: 245/250. Grok v2: 243/250.
- **Short vs cites asymmetry** — `negative_short` consistently outperforms `negative_cites` across models, warranting further investigation of prime format effects.
